summary:
An FMLink profile (republished from ARC Facilities' Inspiring Female Leaders in Facilities Management series) of Brooke Laing, a woman in her early 20s advocating for women in the skilled trades. Laing started college intending to become a diabetes nurse but left after about three weeks, then at her mother's suggestion explored the trades and chose welding. She attended a private trade school, earned multiple welding certifications, and after a long wait joined the pipe union as a dual-trade steamfitter/welder apprentice, working in the trades for several years. Repeated layoffs and the treatment of women in the industry pushed her out; about five months ago she moved into industry media covering manufacturing, working across a network of roughly 11 shows and interviewing people from apprentices to C-suite.

She argues apprenticeship programs now offer structured training and financial assistance that helps employers develop talent, unlike past learn-on-the-job norms. She sees social media, especially Instagram video, as a recruiting and teaching channel for young welders, and notes persistent stigma that women do not belong in the trades. She describes limited high school trades exposure (only auto shop) and a generational cycle in which her predecessors were pushed toward college and IT over trades, creating roughly a decade of skilled trades shortage that her generation is beginning to reverse.

On facilities management, she frames in-house facilities teams and outside skilled tradespeople as complementary, especially for institutional knowledge transfer, which she likens to a "broken telephone" where each handoff loses detail. She recounts a hospital project replacing a leaking underground diesel tank serving the backup generator, leaking five to six liters a day, replaced with two above-ground storage tanks. Work required about a month to secure approval for a temporary generator and scheduling around the dialysis wing. Her advice: ask as many questions as possible.
